1) leptin is present in the stomach, 2) leptin is released from the stomach in response to feeding and fasting, 3) leptin is involved in the regulation of food intake.
gastric leptin is a protein that can be mobilized in response either to food intake or to satiety factors and could participate in the regulation of food intake.
leptin is produced by gastric cells, in particular by endocrine cells of the stomach, and that this protein is mobilized in response both to short-term and long-term changes in the nutritional state.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of leptin in the short-term modulation of food intake.
the role of gastric leptin in the regulation of food intake and energy balance, and the possible involvement of this protein in gastrointestinal diseases such as obesity and diabetes.
the identification of the mechanisms of action of leptin on the digestive system and the role of this protein on the short-term regulation (satiety) of food intake.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stomach produces a protein, leptin, which is mobilized after feeding and is involved in the short-term satiation.
leptin is a satiety factor, which is secreted by the stomach, and which is sensitive to the energy content of a meal.

leptin, as a signal of energy stores, could be considered as a "metabolic" hormone, which, by acting in collaboration with the "satiety" peptides, participates in the regulation of food intake and energy balance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
gastric leptin is a putative satiation factor that is released from the stomach in response to food ingestion.
leptin produced by stomach is an important factor in the short-term satiation and in the regulation of energy balance, in collaboration with other satiety signals, such as cholecysokinin.

leptin is a hormone produced by the stomach, which has a role in short-term control of food intake, and which is involved in the regulation of gastric function, in particular in controlling the gastric emptying rate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
gastric leptin is a key factor in the regulation of energy balance, and that its action on food intake is exerted through a direct pathway, involving leptin receptor activation on the gastric mucosa.
